questions.q: Which group reagent is used for CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>, SO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>, S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>, S<sup>2-</sup> and NO<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup>?
questions.expl: CO3(2-), SO3(2-), S2O3(2-), S2- and NO2- make up the classic dilute acid group: dilute HCl or dilute H2SO4 is strong enough to liberate their characteristic gases without needing concentrated acid.

questions.q: Which of these anions needs the concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> group reagent (not dilute)?
questions.expl: Cl- does not react with dilute acid at all. It only releases HCl gas with the concentrated H2SO4 group reagent, alongside Br-, I-, NO3- and a few others.

questions.q: Which of these anions is tested independently, with no common group reagent?
questions.expl: Sulphate gives no gas with dilute or concentrated acid, so it cannot be placed in either acid group. It is confirmed independently with BaCl2, which gives a white BaSO4 precipitate insoluble in acids.

questions.q: Why does LiHCO<sub>3</sub> never appear as a solid?
options: Alkali metal bicarbonates exist only in solution
questions.expl: LiHCO3 is stable only in aqueous solution. As soon as you try to isolate it as a dry solid it decomposes back into Li2CO3, CO2 and water, so it is never seen as a solid.

questions.q: PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup>, CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> and MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> belong to which group?
questions.expl: Phosphate, chromate and permanganate do not share a common acid-group reagent. Each is confirmed by its own distinctive precipitate or color reaction, so they are grouped as independent anions.

questions.q: Bicarbonates of alkali metals (except Li) are generally found:
options: Only in solution, not as isolable solids
questions.expl: Like lithium bicarbonate, the bicarbonates of Na, K, Rb and Cs are only stable while dissolved. Attempting to isolate any of them as a solid causes decomposition to the carbonate, water and CO2.

questions.q: CO<sub>2</sub> is passed into lime water until in large excess. What happens to the initial milkiness?
questions.expl: Excess CO2 converts insoluble CaCO3 into soluble calcium bicarbonate, Ca(HCO3)2, so the milkiness that first appears clears up again.

questions.q: Which of these gases is non-reducing and will NOT decolorize acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>?
questions.expl: Carbon in CO2 is already fully oxidized (+4), so it has no reducing power left and cannot decolorize acidified KMnO4, unlike SO2, H2S or NO2.

questions.q: Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + AgNO<sub>3</sub> gives a white precipitate that reversibly converts into:
questions.expl: Freshly formed white Ag2CO3 is thermally unstable and readily loses CO2, converting into brown Ag2O.

questions.q: Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + HgCl<sub>2</sub> gives which colored precipitate?
questions.expl: Na2CO3 with HgCl2 forms basic mercuric carbonate, which is reddish brown.

questions.q: Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + CuSO<sub>4</sub> gives which colored precipitate?
questions.expl: Na2CO3 with CuSO4 forms basic copper carbonate, a green precipitate.

questions.q: Which cations give NO precipitate with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, even though they DO precipitate with Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>?
questions.expl: Calcium, strontium and barium bicarbonates are soluble enough that they do not exceed their Ksp with NaHCO3, while their much less soluble normal carbonates readily precipitate with Na2CO3.

questions.q: Which indicator fails to indicate the neutralization endpoint of NaHCO<sub>3</sub>?
questions.expl: Phenolphthalein changes color at the CO3(2-)/HCO3- transition, not at the HCO3-/H2CO3 one, so it cannot mark the endpoint of a pure bicarbonate titration.

questions.q: The final (2nd) equivalence point of a Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> titration is indicated by:
questions.expl: The second equivalence point (HCO3- converting to H2CO3) falls in acidic pH territory, which matches methyl oranges color-change range rather than phenolphthaleins.

questions.q: CO<sub>2</sub>/CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup> is passed through acidified orange K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>. What is observed?
questions.expl: CO2 and carbonate ions have no reducing power, so they cannot convert orange Cr2O7(2-) into green Cr3+; the dichromate color stays unchanged.

questions.q: Any acid stronger than which acid will react with NaHCO<sub>3</sub> to release CO<sub>2</sub>?
questions.expl: Carbonic acid, H2CO3, is such a weak acid that essentially any acid stronger than it, even acetic acid, will displace and release CO2 from a bicarbonate.

questions.q: NaHCO<sub>3</sub> heated strongly gives:
questions.expl: On strong heating, sodium bicarbonate decomposes into sodium carbonate, water vapor and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + Hg<sub>2</sub>(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> gives a yellow precipitate that, on standing, converts to:
questions.expl: The initial yellow mercurous carbonate precipitate is unstable and decomposes on standing into black Hg2O and CO2.

questions.q: BaSO<sub>3</sub> is normally insoluble, but it dissolves readily in:
options: An oxidizing medium, or in conc. HCl
questions.expl: Sulphite salts react readily with acid because sulphurous acid (H2SO3) is weak and unstable, so it decomposes and releases SO2 as it forms; concentrated HCl or an oxidizing acid both drive this dissolution effectively.

questions.q: The group reagent test for a sulphite salt liberates which gas?
questions.expl: The dilute acid group reagent liberates SO2 gas, recognizable by its sharp, choking smell.

questions.q: Sulphite + AgNO<sub>3</sub> forms a clear solution which, on boiling, gives:
questions.expl: Sulphite reacts with AgNO3 to give a clear solution that, on boiling, deposits a white precipitate of Ag2SO3, which is itself a reducing agent.

questions.q: On further boiling, Ag<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> decomposes into:
questions.expl: On further prolonged boiling, Ag2SO3 disproportionates, giving metallic silver, SO2 gas and sulphate ions.

questions.q: Aldehydes and methyl ketones react with NaHSO<sub>3</sub> to form:
options: A white crystalline bisulphite addition compound
questions.expl: The electrophilic carbonyl carbon of aldehydes and methyl ketones is attacked by the nucleophilic sulphite ion, forming a crystalline bisulphite addition compound.

questions.q: A sulphite salt treated with Zn/HCl (or Fe/HCl) produces:
questions.expl: Nascent hydrogen generated by Zn or Fe with HCl reduces sulphite all the way down to H2S gas.

questions.q: In an oxidizing medium, the white Ag<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> precipitate converts to:
questions.expl: An oxidizing medium converts the sulphite in Ag2SO3 up to sulphate, giving white Ag2SO4.

questions.q: Insoluble BaSO<sub>4</sub> also dissolves in conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> because it forms:
options: It never dissolves in any acid
questions.expl: Concentrated H2SO4 protonates sulphate to the soluble bisulphate ion, which is why even the notoriously insoluble BaSO4 dissolves in it.

questions.q: Which of the following thiosulphates is INSOLUBLE?
questions.expl: Silver binds thiosulphate strongly enough to form an insoluble white salt, unlike the freely soluble alkali metal and ammonium thiosulphates.

questions.q: The group test for thiosulphate with dilute acid gives:
options: Sulphur precipitate AND SO<sub>2</sub> gas together
questions.expl: Dilute acid causes unstable thiosulphuric acid to disproportionate, producing a turbid precipitate of free sulphur together with SO2 gas.

questions.q: White Ag<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> reacting with excess Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> gives:
questions.expl: Excess thiosulphate acts as a ligand, wrapping around Ag+ to form the soluble complex ion [Ag(S2O3)2]3-, the same chemistry used in photographic fixer.

questions.q: Ag<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> reacting with water on boiling turns into:
questions.expl: On boiling with water, the white Ag2S2O3 hydrolyzes and decomposes, depositing black Ag2S.

questions.q: Unlike AgCl, the black Ag<sub>2</sub>S formed from thiosulphate is, when treated with NH<sub>3</sub>:
questions.expl: The Ag2S formed from thiosulphate is far less soluble than AgCl, so unlike AgCl it does not dissolve in ammonia solution.

questions.q: Thiosulphate + FeCl<sub>3</sub> gives which colored precipitate?
questions.expl: Fe3+ forms a violet thiosulphato complex with thiosulphate ions.

questions.q: Adding excess Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> to the violet Fe<sub>2</sub>(S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> precipitate gives:
questions.expl: Excess thiosulphate reduces the violet Fe3+ complex, converting it into a green iron(II) thiosulphate species.

questions.q: Thiosulphate decolorizes the blue-black starch-iodine complex by converting I<sub>2</sub> into:
questions.expl: Thiosulphate reduces iodine to iodide while itself being oxidized to tetrathionate, which is why it decolorizes the blue-black starch-iodine complex.

questions.q: Unstable H<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> decomposes to:
questions.expl: Free thiosulphuric acid is too unstable to exist for long and immediately breaks down into water, SO2 and sulphur.

questions.q: Thiosulphate + Pb(OAc)<sub>2</sub> gives a white ppt → excess reagent gives a soluble complex → water then gives:
questions.expl: As with silver, the soluble lead-thiosulphate complex hydrolyzes on standing in water to deposit black PbS.

questions.q: CN<sup>-</sup> + Pb<sup>2+</sup> gives white PbSO<sub>3</sub>; that same solution + FeCl<sub>3</sub> gives what colored precipitate?
questions.expl: This item mixes labels that do not quite belong together (cyanide and lead sulphite alongside an iron reaction) and looks like a data entry slip rather than a clean chemistry fact. The color described, blood-red, is the signature of the thiocyanate test: Fe3+ reacting with SCN- forms the deep red complex ion [Fe(SCN)]2+. Treat this one with caution and consider checking the original source.

questions.q: The group reagent test for a sulphide salt liberates which gas?
questions.expl: The dilute acid group reagent liberates H2S gas from a sulphide salt, recognizable by its rotten-egg smell.

questions.q: Which THREE sulphides need aqua regia (not just conc. HNO<sub>3</sub>) to dissolve?
questions.expl: HgS, CoS and NiS are so insoluble and chemically inert that even concentrated HNO3 cannot break them down; only aqua regia, with its combination of oxidizing power and complexing chloride, can dissolve them.

questions.q: The nitroprusside test for a soluble sulphide salt gives which color?
questions.expl: Soluble sulphide reacting with sodium nitroprusside gives a characteristic, if fleeting, violet color.

questions.q: The nitroprusside test fails for:
questions.expl: The nitroprusside test needs an appreciable S2- ion concentration in solution. Free H2S gas ionizes so little that the S2- level is too low to give a visible response.

questions.q: The methylene blue test is specific for detecting:
questions.expl: Methylene blue, formed from sulphide reacting with an aromatic amine and Fe3+, is a specific and sensitive confirmatory test for H2S.

questions.q: Sulphide + Pb(OAc)<sub>2</sub> gives black PbS, which on treatment with H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> becomes:
questions.expl: Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes black PbS up to white PbSO4.

questions.q: Group 1 (alkali metal) sulphides are generally:
questions.expl: Group 1 (alkali metal) sulphides such as Na2S and K2S are freely soluble in water, unlike most transition metal sulphides.

questions.q: Aqueous solutions of group 1/2 sulphides are basic due to:
questions.expl: The sulphide ion is the conjugate base of a very weak acid (H2S), so it hydrolyzes in water to give HS- and OH-, making the solution basic.

questions.q: Cr<sub>2</sub>S<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O gives a green precipitate of:
questions.expl: Cr2S3 is the salt of a weak base (Cr3+) and a weak acid (S2-), so it undergoes complete hydrolysis in water, releasing green Cr(OH)3 and H2S gas.

questions.q: Sulphide salt + Cd(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> gives which colored precipitate?
questions.expl: Cadmium sulphide is a bright yellow precipitate, one of the more memorable confirmatory colors in qualitative analysis.

questions.q: The group test gas for a nitrite salt is colorless NO, which then:
questions.expl: The colorless NO gas released by the nitrite group test is rapidly oxidized by atmospheric oxygen into reddish-brown NO2.

questions.q: The nitrite ring test uses which acid strength/conditions?
questions.expl: Nitrous acid is unstable enough on its own that the nitrite ring test works with cold, dilute H2SO4, unlike the nitrate ring test which needs concentrated acid and heat.

questions.q: Using conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> instead of dilute in the nitrite ring test would:
options: Further oxidize NO to NO<sub>2</sub>, spoiling the test
Prevent the ring from forming entirely
questions.expl: Concentrated H2SO4 is too strongly oxidizing, converting the NO needed to form the brown ring further into NO2 and destroying the test.

questions.q: For the nitrite + KI + starch test, acidification must use:
questions.expl: A mineral acid like HCl or H2SO4 would itself oxidize the iodide being tested for. Acetic acid liberates HNO2 from the nitrite without oxidizing the iodide, keeping the test clean.

questions.q: A nitrite salt heated with NH<sub>4</sub>Cl gives which gas?
questions.expl: Ammonium and nitrite ions comproportionate on heating, producing pure nitrogen gas and water, a classic laboratory method for preparing N2.

questions.q: The Griess–Ilosvay test for nitrite produces:
questions.expl: The Griess-Ilosvay reaction diazotizes an aromatic amine with nitrous acid and then couples it to a second reagent, producing a colored azo dye.

questions.q: All nitrites are soluble except:
questions.expl: Silver nitrite is the one common insoluble nitrite salt; alkali metal and ammonium nitrites are all soluble.

questions.q: A nitrite salt treated with Zn-NaOH or Al-NaOH liberates which gas?
questions.expl: Nascent hydrogen produced by Zn or Al with NaOH reduces nitrite to ammonia gas.

questions.q: White reducing AgNO<sub>2</sub> reacting with acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> turns the KMnO<sub>4</sub>:
questions.expl: Reducing AgNO2 reduces the deep purple permanganate ion down to colorless Mn2+.

questions.q: A nitrite salt gets oxidized by MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>, Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> or halates, converting itself into:
questions.expl: Oxidizing agents such as permanganate, dichromate or halates push nitrite up to the more oxidized nitrate ion.

questions.q: The group test for nitrate with conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and heat gives:
questions.expl: Heating a nitrate with concentrated H2SO4 decomposes the nitric acid formed in situ, releasing reddish-brown NO2 fumes.

questions.q: Adding Cu chips to the nitrate + conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> test:
questions.expl: Copper reduces the nitric acid generated, producing more NO2 and intensifying the reddish-brown fumes.

questions.q: The nitrate brown ring test requires FeSO<sub>4</sub> in what amount?
questions.expl: The ring test needs a large excess of FeSO4, both to reduce enough nitrate to NO and to have plenty of Fe2+ left over to trap that NO as a brown complex.

questions.q: What is the dual role of FeSO<sub>4</sub> in the nitrate ring test?
questions.expl: Fe2+ plays two roles at once: it reduces NO3- down to NO, and it also complexes that NO as the brown ring compound [Fe(H2O)5(NO)]2+.

questions.q: Which insoluble nitrate is brown in color?
questions.expl: Bismuth oxynitrate, BiONO3, is the classic brown insoluble basic nitrate salt.

questions.q: Insoluble oxo-/hydroxo-nitrate salts dissolve in:
options: Strongly acidic medium, e.g. conc. HNO<sub>3</sub>
questions.expl: Strong acid reverses the hydrolysis that produced these basic or oxo-nitrate salts, protonating them back into solution.

questions.q: The main difference between the nitrate and nitrite ring tests is:
options: Nitrate needs conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + heat + large excess FeSO<sub>4</sub>; nitrite needs only dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, no heat
Nitrate doesn't need FeSO<sub>4</sub> at all
questions.expl: The key procedural difference is concentration and heat: the nitrate ring test needs concentrated H2SO4, heating, and a large excess of FeSO4, while the nitrite ring test needs only cold dilute acid.

questions.q: A nitrate salt treated with Zn-NaOH or Al-NaOH liberates which gas?
questions.expl: Just like nitrite, nitrate is reduced all the way down to ammonia gas by nascent hydrogen from Zn or Al in NaOH.

questions.q: Which of these normally-insoluble chlorides is soluble in conc. HCl?
questions.expl: Cuprous chloride is the one commonly insoluble chloride that redissolves in excess concentrated HCl, forming a soluble chloro complex.

questions.q: The group test: chloride + conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + KCl gives which gas?
questions.expl: The standard chloride group test with concentrated H2SO4 liberates pungent HCl gas.

questions.q: To liberate Cl<sub>2</sub> gas (not just HCl) from a chloride salt, you add:
options: An oxidizer like MnO<sub>2</sub> or PbO<sub>2</sub> with conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
questions.expl: To get free Cl2 gas rather than just HCl, an oxidizing agent such as MnO2 or PbO2 is needed to oxidize the chloride further.

questions.q: White Hg<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> reacting with NH<sub>3</sub> undergoes disproportionation to give:
questions.expl: Mercurous chloride disproportionates with ammonia into white aminomercury(II) chloride plus black metallic mercury, giving an overall grey to black appearance.

questions.q: Which chlorides give a NEGATIVE chromyl chloride test due to significant covalent character?
questions.expl: SnCl4 and HgCl2 are largely covalent rather than ionic, so they do not release enough free Cl- in solution to give a positive chromyl chloride test.

questions.q: The chromyl chloride test cannot be extended to bromide or iodide because:
options: HBr/HI are too easily oxidized under the conditions
Br and I don't form any chlorides
The reaction is simply too slow
questions.expl: The concentrated H2SO4 needed for the test would oxidize bromide or iodide into free Br2 or I2 before chromyl chloride can even form, so the test does not extend to them.

questions.q: A high concentration of Cl<sup>-</sup> is needed for a positive chromyl chloride test because:
options: Excess HCl is needed, since part of it gets oxidized by the CrO<sub>3</sub> formed
Low Cl<sup>-</sup> gives a false positive
Cl<sup>-</sup> only acts as a catalyst
questions.expl: Some of the Cl- is consumed as it gets oxidized by the CrO3 formed during the reaction, so a high chloride concentration is needed to leave enough left over to react.

questions.q: Reddish CrO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> vapor reacting with aqueous KOH gives:
questions.expl: CrO2Cl2 vapor hydrolyzes in aqueous KOH to give the yellow chromate ion, K2CrO4.

questions.q: SnCl<sub>2</sub> reacting with water converts into an insoluble oxychloride:
questions.expl: SnCl2 partially hydrolyzes in water, forming the insoluble basic salt Sn(OH)Cl.

questions.q: All chloride salts are soluble except:
options: AgCl, PbCl<sub>2</sub>, Hg<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, CuCl (and a few oxychlorides)
questions.expl: AgCl, PbCl2, Hg2Cl2 and CuCl, along with a handful of oxychlorides, make up the standard list of chlorides that will not dissolve in water.

questions.q: Chloride + Hg<sub>2</sub>(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> gives a white/yellowish-white precipitate that turns which color with NH<sub>3</sub>?
questions.expl: Just as with Hg2Cl2, ammonia disproportionates the mercury salt into black metallic mercury and a white aminomercury compound.

questions.q: Etard oxidation (toluene + CrO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>) ultimately produces:
questions.expl: In the Etard reaction, the chromium ester intermediate formed from toluene and CrO2Cl2 hydrolyzes to give benzaldehyde, stopping short of the fully oxidized acid.

questions.q: All bromide salts are soluble except:
questions.expl: AgBr, PbBr2, Hg2Br2 and CuBr mirror the insoluble chloride list, since bromide behaves similarly but with somewhat lower solubility.

questions.q: Conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + a bromide salt gives which colored fumes, and why?
questions.expl: Unlike chloride, concentrated H2SO4 is a strong enough oxidizer on its own to liberate free bromine directly from a bromide salt.

questions.q: Orthophosphoric acid (H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>) + bromide gives:
options: Colorless HBr fumes, turning brown only via aerial oxidation
questions.expl: Phosphoric acid is non-oxidizing, so it simply displaces colorless HBr gas; the fumes only turn brown slowly as the HBr is oxidized by air.

questions.q: The fluorescein test converts yellow-orange fluorescein into a bright pink/red dye called:
questions.expl: Liberated bromine substitutes four bromine atoms onto fluorescein, converting the yellow-orange dye into the bright pink Eosin Y.

questions.q: The fluorescein test alone cannot distinguish bromide from iodide because:
options: Eosin (from Br<sub>2</sub>) and erythrosine (from I<sub>2</sub>) are both shades of red/pink
They form the exact same compound
questions.expl: Eosin, formed from bromine, and erythrosine, formed from iodine, are both similar shades of pink to red, so the fluorescein test alone cannot tell the two halides apart.

questions.q: To properly distinguish Br<sup>-</sup> and I<sup>-</sup> in a mixture, chemists use:
options: The layer test with CHCl<sub>3</sub> as solvent
questions.expl: A non-aqueous chloroform layer shows visibly distinct colors for bromine and iodine that are otherwise hard to distinguish in water, allowing the two to be told apart.

questions.q: In the layer test, the halogen X<sub>2</sub>' used must be positioned _____ X in the periodic table to displace it.
questions.expl: To displace a halide, the reagent halogen has to sit above it in the group, since reactivity as an oxidizer decreases going down the group.

questions.q: A bromide salt + F<sub>2</sub> in the layer test gives what colored layer over CHCl<sub>3</sub>?
questions.expl: Fluorine, sitting above bromine, displaces it, and the liberated Br2 dissolves in the chloroform layer to give a reddish-brown color.

questions.q: White PbBr<sub>2</sub> is:
options: Insoluble in cold water, but dissolves in hot water
questions.expl: Lead bromides solubility is strongly temperature dependent, staying undissolved in cold water but dissolving readily once heated.

questions.q: Bromide salt + MnO<sub>2</sub> + conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> gives:
questions.expl: MnO2 is an oxidizer strong enough, together with concentrated H2SO4, to liberate intense reddish-brown Br2 fumes from a bromide salt.

questions.q: All iodide salts are soluble except:
options: AgI, PbI<sub>2</sub>, Hg<sub>2</sub>I<sub>2</sub>, CuI, BiI<sub>3</sub>, HgI<sub>2</sub>, BiOI
questions.expl: AgI, PbI2, Hg2I2, CuI, BiI3, HgI2 and BiOI make up an even longer insoluble list than chloride or bromide, reflecting iodides greater tendency to form insoluble salts.

questions.q: Conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + an iodide salt gives violet fumes plus how many total gaseous products?
questions.expl: Concentrated H2SO4 both liberates HI and, being a strong enough oxidant, further oxidizes some of it to I2 and SO2, with water also formed, giving four gaseous products in total.

questions.q: Nessler's reagent, used to test for ammonia, has the formula:
questions.expl: Nesslers reagent is potassium tetraiodomercurate(II), K2[HgI4], prepared in alkaline solution.

questions.q: Nessler's reagent + NH<sub>3</sub> gives which colored precipitate?
questions.expl: Trace ammonia reacting with Nesslers reagent gives a distinctive brown precipitate known as the iodide of Millons base, sensitive enough to detect very low levels of NH3.

questions.q: I<sup>-</sup> + Hg<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup> (mercurous) initially gives which colored precipitate?
questions.expl: Iodide with excess mercurous ion first gives a green precipitate of Hg2I2, which with further excess iodide disproportionates into HgI2 and metallic mercury.

questions.q: I<sub>2</sub> is well known to catalyze the redox reaction between:
questions.expl: Iodine or iodide is a well known catalyst for the otherwise sluggish redox reaction between ceric ion and arsenite.

questions.q: Which of these does NOT liberate I<sub>2</sub> from an iodide salt?
questions.expl: NaCl is simply another halide salt with no oxidizing power, so it cannot liberate I2 from an iodide the way chlorine or an oxidizing agent can.

questions.q: Yellow PbI<sub>2</sub> (insoluble in water) becomes soluble in:
questions.expl: Excess iodide acts as a ligand, complexing lead into the soluble tetraiodoplumbate ion, PbI4(2-), redissolving the yellow precipitate.

questions.q: I<sup>-</sup> + Hg<sup>2+</sup> gives which colored precipitate first?
questions.expl: Mercuric ion with iodide first gives a bright scarlet-red precipitate of HgI2, which dissolves in excess iodide to the colorless complex [HgI4]2-.

questions.q: Iodine vapor's electrophilic substitution on fluorescein at room temperature is:
options: Too weak to give a distinct pink reaction
questions.expl: Iodine is a much weaker electrophile than bromine, so its substitution onto fluorescein at room temperature is too slow and weak to give a clear pink reaction.

questions.q: Which of these sulphates are completely insoluble?
questions.expl: Ag2SO4, PbSO4, BaSO4 and SrSO4 make up the standard list of sulphates that are essentially insoluble in water.

questions.q: BaSO<sub>4</sub> dissolves ONLY in:
options: It never dissolves in any acid
questions.expl: BaSO4 resists ordinary acids entirely and dissolves only in very concentrated H2SO4, which protonates it into the soluble bisulphate, Ba(HSO4)2.

questions.q: HgSO<sub>4</sub>.HgO is what colored precipitate?
questions.expl: HgSO4.HgO, a basic mercuric sulphate, is a characteristic yellow precipitate.

questions.q: Cr(OH)SO<sub>4</sub> is what colored precipitate?
questions.expl: Cr(OH)SO4, basic chromium sulphate, is a green precipitate.

questions.q: White PbSO<sub>4</sub>, insoluble even in hot water, dissolves in:
questions.expl: Like BaSO4, lead sulphate is inert to most acids and dissolves only in concentrated H2SO4, forming the soluble bisulphate Pb(HSO4)2.

questions.q: CaSO<sub>4</sub> and HgSO<sub>4</sub> are best described as:
questions.expl: CaSO4 and HgSO4 sit in between the freely soluble sulphates (like Na2SO4) and the essentially insoluble ones (like BaSO4), so they are best described as only slightly soluble.

questions.q: Sulphate salt + HgCl<sub>2</sub> gives which colored precipitate?
questions.expl: Sulphate reacting with HgCl2 gives a yellow basic mercury sulphate precipitate, HgSO4.H2O.

questions.q: White BaSO<sub>4</sub> (from BaCl<sub>2</sub> + sulphate) is insoluble even in:
options: Dilute/conc. HCl or HNO<sub>3</sub>, dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, or halogen water
It's actually soluble in all of these
questions.expl: BaSO4 is famously unreactive toward essentially all common acids and oxidizers, which is exactly why it is used as a reliable confirmatory and gravimetric test for sulphate.

questions.q: A salt gives a purple color in its dry state. Which ion is most likely responsible?
questions.expl: A deep purple color in the dry salt strongly points to permanganate, MnO4-.

questions.q: Hydrated salts of Mn<sup>2+</sup> and Co<sup>2+</sup> are typically what color?
questions.expl: Hydrated manganese(II) and cobalt(II) salts are both characteristically pale pink.

questions.q: A blue-colored aqueous solution most likely contains which ion?
questions.expl: A blue aqueous solution is the classic signature of hydrated copper(II) ions.

questions.q: A green solution could contain which of these ions?
questions.expl: Nickel(II), iron(II) and chromium(III) can all give green solutions, so color alone cannot distinguish between them without further confirmatory tests.

questions.q: An ammoniacal, pungent, urinal-like smell from a salt indicates the presence of:
questions.expl: A pungent, ammoniacal smell, especially on warming or making alkaline, indicates ammonium ion.

questions.q: A light, fluffy powder texture in a salt suggests the presence of:
questions.expl: Carbonates (and bicarbonates) commonly form light, fluffy, low-density solids.

questions.q: If a deliquescent salt turns colored as it absorbs moisture, it may be:
questions.expl: Copper nitrate and ferric chloride are both colored as well as deliquescent, so as they absorb atmospheric moisture the developing color becomes visible.

questions.q: What color does Na<sup>+</sup> impart to a Bunsen flame?
questions.expl: Sodium ions give the well known intense golden-yellow flame color.

questions.q: What color does K<sup>+</sup> impart to a flame?
questions.expl: Potassium ions give a pale lilac to violet flame color.

questions.q: What color does Li<sup>+</sup> impart to a flame?
questions.expl: Lithium ions give a characteristic crimson-red flame color.

questions.q: Sr<sup>2+</sup> gives which flame color?
questions.expl: Strontium ions give a crimson-red flame color, similar to lithium, so other tests are needed to tell them apart.

questions.q: Ba<sup>2+</sup> gives which flame color?
questions.expl: Barium ions give an apple-green flame color.

questions.q: Which two metals give NO flame test color at all?
questions.expl: Beryllium and magnesium do not undergo the same easily visible electronic transitions in a flame as the alkali and heavier alkaline earth metals, so neither gives a characteristic flame color.

questions.q: When Na<sup>+</sup> and K<sup>+</sup> are both present, what masks the potassium color to the naked eye?
options: They cancel out to give no color
questions.expl: Sodiums flame emission is so much more intense than potassiums that it swamps the faint lilac potassium color to the naked eye.

questions.q: Viewed through blue (cobalt) glass, how do the Na<sup>+</sup> and K<sup>+</sup> flame colors appear?
options: Na disappears, K shows a crimson red flame
questions.expl: Cobalt glass absorbs sodiums yellow light, letting potassiums much weaker crimson-red emission show through.

questions.q: What is the role of concentrated HCl in the flame test?
options: Provides H<sup>+</sup> ions for the flame
Converts the salt into a volatile cationic chloride
questions.expl: Concentrated HCl converts the sample into its chloride salt, which is volatile enough to vaporize readily in the flame and produce a strong emission.

questions.q: The characteristic yellow flame color of sodium arises from which electronic transition?
questions.expl: The yellow sodium line comes from a valence electron being excited from the 3s to the 3p orbital and then releasing that energy as light on returning to the ground state.

questions.q: Pb<sup>2+</sup> gives which flame color?
questions.expl: Lead ions give a pale bluish or greyish flame color.

questions.q: A heated, transparent borax bead is chemically composed of:
questions.expl: On heating, borax loses its water of crystallization and decomposes into a fused glassy mixture of sodium metaborate and boric anhydride.

questions.q: In the oxidizing flame (hot), a chromium (Cr<sup>3+</sup>) borax bead appears:
questions.expl: In the hot oxidizing flame, a chromium bead is yellow to green, reflecting a higher chromium oxidation state stabilized under oxidizing conditions.

questions.q: In the oxidizing flame (cold), the chromium borax bead appears:
questions.expl: On cooling in the oxidizing flame, the chromium bead settles into a green color, closer to Cr2O3.

questions.q: In the reducing flame, a chromium borax bead stays which color (both hot and cold)?
questions.expl: In the reducing flame, the chromium bead stays green in both its hot and cold state.

questions.q: A manganese (Mn<sup>2+</sup>) borax bead in the oxidizing flame (hot) is:
questions.expl: In the hot oxidizing flame, manganese forms a violet bead, reflecting a higher, colored oxidation state.

questions.q: In the reducing flame, the manganese borax bead becomes:
questions.expl: In the reducing flame, manganese is reduced to Mn2+, giving a colorless to grey bead.

questions.q: An iron (Fe<sup>3+</sup>) borax bead in the oxidizing flame (hot) is:
questions.expl: In the hot oxidizing flame, iron forms a yellowish-brown bead.

questions.q: In the reducing flame, the iron borax bead turns green or bottle-green due to the formation of:
questions.expl: The green to bottle-green color seen in the reducing flame comes from iron being reduced to the ferrous, Fe2+, state.

questions.q: A cobalt (Co<sup>2+</sup>) borax bead is which color in the oxidizing flame?
questions.expl: Cobalt gives a characteristic blue bead in the oxidizing flame, a color so intense and specific it is used as a comparison standard.

questions.q: A nickel (Ni<sup>2+</sup>) borax bead in the oxidizing flame (hot) is:
questions.expl: Nickel gives a violet bead in the hot oxidizing flame.

questions.q: A copper (Cu<sup>2+</sup>) borax bead in the oxidizing flame (hot) is:
questions.expl: Copper gives a blue bead in the hot oxidizing flame.

questions.q: In the reducing flame (cold), the copper borax bead turns opaque brown-red due to:
questions.expl: In the cold reducing flame, copper is reduced all the way to metallic copper, which deposits as an opaque brown-red color in the bead.

questions.q: The borax bead test is characteristically given by transition metal ions that:
options: Have unpaired electrons and form colored compounds
questions.expl: The borax bead color comes from d-d electronic transitions in transition metal ions that carry unpaired d electrons; ions without unpaired d electrons do not give this color.

questions.q: Alums also show the swelling characteristic of borax on heating, but on strong heating they:
options: Also form a transparent glassy bead
Convert into an amorphous powder (unlike borax)
questions.expl: Alums also swell on initial heating from losing their water of crystallization, but unlike borax they do not fuse into a clear glass bead on strong heating, instead breaking down into an amorphous white powder.

questions.q: Which of the following gives a positive borax bead test?
questions.expl: Manganese in the +3 oxidation state is the one that gives a positive violet borax bead color among the options listed.

questions.q: The borax bead swells up before forming a clear bead because of:
questions.expl: The initial swelling and puffing of the bead comes from the rapid, sudden loss of boraxs water of hydration as it is first heated.

questions.q: What is the chemical formula of microcosmic salt?
questions.expl: Microcosmic salt is sodium ammonium hydrogen phosphate, Na(NH4)HPO4 with four molecules of water of crystallization.

questions.q: On strong heating, microcosmic salt decomposes to form a glassy bead of:
questions.expl: On strong heating, microcosmic salt loses water and ammonia, leaving behind a glassy bead of sodium metaphosphate, NaPO3.

questions.q: In the oxidizing flame, the sodium metaphosphate bead reacts with a transition metal oxide to form:
questions.expl: The metaphosphate bead combines with a transition metal oxide to form a colored mixed phosphate, in direct analogy to how borax forms a mixed metaborate.

questions.q: Initial heating of microcosmic salt produces a crackling/decrepitation sound because it is:
questions.expl: The crackling, decrepitation sound heard during initial heating comes from the rapid escape of the salts water of crystallization.

questions.q: A 'red scale' observed in the charcoal cavity test suggests the presence of:
questions.expl: A red scale in the charcoal cavity, from a thin film of copper or copper oxide, is a classic indicator of copper.

questions.q: A metallic bead with a yellow incrustation in the charcoal cavity test suggests:
questions.expl: A metallic bead surrounded by a yellow incrustation of lead oxide is characteristic of lead.

questions.q: A residue that is yellow when hot but turns white on cooling (with no bead) suggests:
questions.expl: Zinc oxide is yellow while hot but turns white on cooling, and zinc is too volatile to form a lasting metallic bead, matching this description.

questions.q: A white infusible residue in the charcoal cavity test could indicate which group of cations?
options: Zn<sup>2+</sup>, Al<sup>3+</sup>, Mg<sup>2+</sup>, Ba<sup>2+</sup>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Sn<sup>2+</sup>
questions.expl: Zinc, aluminum, magnesium, barium, calcium and tin all give white, infusible oxide residues in the charcoal cavity rather than colored residues or metal beads.

questions.q: The cobalt nitrate test is performed only on residues that were, in the charcoal cavity test:
questions.expl: The cobalt nitrate test, which checks for a further color change, is only meaningfully applied to residues that were already white and infusible.

questions.q: Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + CoO on heating gives which characteristic color?
questions.expl: Alumina reacting with cobalt oxide on heating gives the deep blue color known as Thenards blue.

questions.q: ZnO + CoO on heating gives which characteristic color?
questions.expl: Zinc oxide reacting with cobalt oxide on heating gives the green color known as Rinmanns green.

questions.q: MgO + CoO on heating gives which characteristic color?
questions.expl: Magnesium oxide reacting with cobalt oxide on heating gives a pink color.

questions.q: SnO + CoO on heating gives which characteristic color?
questions.expl: Tin oxide reacting with cobalt oxide on heating gives a bluish-green, or azure, color.

questions.q: In the dry heat test, a residue that is yellow when hot but white when cold indicates:
questions.expl: Zinc oxide is famously thermochromic: bright yellow while hot but turning white again on cooling.

questions.q: In the dry heat test, a residue that is red when cold but black when hot indicates:
questions.expl: Ferric oxide is reddish when cold and darkens to near-black when strongly heated.

questions.q: If NO solid residue at all is obtained in the dry heat test, the cation is likely:
questions.expl: Ammonium (and similarly volatile, non-metallic cations like phosphonium) decompose or sublime away completely on heating, leaving no residue at all.

questions.q: A yellow-brown residue when hot that turns yellow when cold indicates:
questions.expl: Tin(IV) oxide and bismuth(III) oxide both give a yellow-brown residue when hot that settles to yellow on cooling.

questions.q: Which reagents commonly give white sublimates on dry heating?
questions.expl: HgCl2, Hg2Cl2, As2O3, Sb2O3 and ammonium salts are all volatile enough to sublime, condensing as a white deposit on cooler glass.

questions.q: A black sublimate on dry heating is characteristic of:
questions.expl: Mercury sulphide sublimes to give a black (or, under some conditions, red vermilion) deposit.

questions.q: A yellow sublimate on dry heating could indicate:
questions.expl: Mercuric iodide and arsenic trisulphide both give a yellow sublimate on heating.

questions.q: If N<sub>2</sub> gas (not N<sub>2</sub>O) is evolved on heating a salt, this suggests:
options: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> combined with a non-oxidizing anion
NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> combined with an oxidizing anion (e.g. NO<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup>, Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup>)
questions.expl: When the ammonium ion is paired with an oxidizing anion like nitrite or dichromate, that anion oxidizes the ammonium nitrogen in the process, so all the nitrogen ends up leaving as N2 rather than as NH3.

questions.q: If NH<sub>3</sub> gas is evolved on heating a salt, this suggests:
options: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> combined with an oxidizing anion
NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> combined with a non-oxidizing anion (e.g. Cl<sup>-</sup>, CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>, SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>)
questions.expl: When ammonium is paired with a non-oxidizing anion like chloride, carbonate or sulphate, no internal oxidation happens, so the ammonium is simply decomposed and released as NH3 gas.

questions.q: Which alkali metal carbonate is the one exception that DOES decompose on heating?
questions.expl: Lithium carbonate is the one alkali metal carbonate that decomposes on strong heating, since lithiums small size and high charge density destabilize the carbonate the way larger alkali carbonates are not affected.

questions.q: Heating white lead carbonate (2PbCO<sub>3</sub>·Pb(OH)<sub>2</sub>) at 350°C gives which red-orange product?
questions.expl: White basic lead carbonate decomposes at moderate temperature into the red-orange mixed oxide known as red lead, Pb3O4.

questions.q: On strong heating, pink hydrated CoCl<sub>2</sub>·6H<sub>2</sub>O eventually loses all its water to give anhydrous CoCl<sub>2</sub>, which is:
questions.expl: Once all its water of hydration is driven off, anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue, in contrast to the pink hydrated form.

questions.q: 'Swells' as an action-of-heat observation is characteristic of:
questions.expl: Both borates and alums characteristically swell and puff up on heating because of the rapid loss of their water of crystallization.

questions.q: What is the group reagent for Group I cations (Pb<sup>2+</sup>, Ag<sup>+</sup>, Hg<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup>)?
questions.expl: Lead, silver and mercurous ions are precipitated as insoluble chlorides by dilute HCl, defining Group I.

questions.q: What is the group reagent for Group II cations?
questions.expl: Group II cations are precipitated as sulphides in an acidic medium, where the low sulphide ion concentration favors only the least soluble sulphides.

questions.q: Fe<sup>3+</sup>, Cr<sup>3+</sup>, and Al<sup>3+</sup> are precipitated as hydroxides by NH<sub>4</sub>OH + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl — which group is this?
questions.expl: Iron(III), chromium(III) and aluminum are precipitated together as hydroxides by ammonium hydroxide buffered with ammonium chloride, defining Group III.

questions.q: Which cations belong to Group IV, precipitated by NH<sub>4</sub>OH + H<sub>2</sub>S?
questions.expl: Zinc, manganese, cobalt and nickel are precipitated as sulphides under the more basic conditions of ammonium hydroxide plus H2S, since their sulphides need a higher sulphide ion concentration to precipitate.

questions.q: Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Ba<sup>2+</sup>, and Sr<sup>2+</sup> are precipitated as white carbonates using which group reagent?
questions.expl: Calcium, barium and strontium are precipitated as white carbonates using ammonium carbonate buffered with ammonium chloride, defining Group V.

questions.q: What is the group reagent for Mg<sup>2+</sup> (Group VI), which gives white Mg(NH<sub>4</sub>)PO<sub>4</sub>?
questions.expl: Magnesium is precipitated as white magnesium ammonium phosphate using a combined reagent of ammonium chloride, ammonium hydroxide and ammonium hydrogen phosphate.

questions.q: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (Group Zero) is detected using which reagent, releasing NH<sub>3</sub> gas?
questions.expl: Ammonium ion is detected by warming the sample with NaOH, which releases pungent ammonia gas that turns red litmus blue.

questions.q: Why is NH<sub>4</sub>Cl added along with NH<sub>4</sub>OH before Group III precipitation?
options: To increase OH<sup>-</sup> concentration for complete precipitation
To lower OH<sup>-</sup> concentration (common-ion effect) so only very-low-K<sub>sp</sub> hydroxides precipitate
To dissolve the Group III hydroxides again
questions.expl: Ammonium chloride suppresses the ionization of ammonium hydroxide through the common-ion effect, keeping the hydroxide ion concentration low enough that only the very-low-Ksp Group III hydroxides precipitate, while Group IV and V cations stay in solution.

questions.q: Before testing with the Group III reagent, the solution is boiled with dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> in order to:
options: Oxidize Fe<sup>2+</sup> to Fe<sup>3+</sup> so it precipitates completely as Fe(OH)<sub>3</sub>
questions.expl: Boiling with dilute HNO3 ensures all the iron present is oxidized to Fe3+, since Fe(OH)2 is more soluble than Fe(OH)3 and would not precipitate completely as part of Group III.

questions.q: Why can NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> NOT be used in place of NH<sub>4</sub>Cl for Group III precipitation?
options: NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> can oxidize Mn<sup>2+</sup> to Mn<sup>3+</sup>, causing unwanted Mn(OH)<sub>3</sub> precipitation
It precipitates Group I cations by mistake
questions.expl: Nitrate ion can oxidize Mn2+ up to Mn3+, causing manganese hydroxide to precipitate along with Group III by mistake, which is why the non-oxidizing ammonium chloride is used instead.

questions.q: What condition determines whether a salt precipitates from solution?
questions.expl: A precipitate forms only once the ion product, Qsp, exceeds the solubility product, Ksp, of that compound.

questions.q: Which zone of the Bunsen flame is the hottest, at roughly 1550°C?
options: Just above the tip of the inner cone
questions.expl: The zone just above the tip of the inner cone is where unburnt gas and air mix and combust most completely, making it the hottest part of the flame at around 1550C.

questions.q: Which zone of the Bunsen flame is used for reducing oxides to the free metal?
options: The upper reducing zone (rich in carbon)
questions.expl: The upper zone of the flame is rich in unburnt carbon particles, which can strip oxygen from metal oxides, reducing them toward the free metal.

questions.q: The lower oxidizing zone of the flame is generally used for:
options: The borax-bead test and microcosmic salt test
questions.expl: The cooler, oxygen-rich lower mantle provides the steady, well-aerated heat needed for the borax bead and microcosmic salt color tests.

questions.q: What is the general formula of an open-chain (acyclic) alkane?
questions.expl: Alkanes contain only single C–C and C–H bonds (zero degree of unsaturation), which fixes the general formula at CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

questions.q: A carbon atom bonded to exactly three other carbon atoms is classified as:
questions.expl: Classification of a carbon (1°/2°/3°/4°) depends only on how many other carbons it is directly bonded to — three neighbouring carbons makes it tertiary.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of neopentane, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>C?
questions.expl: The longest chain through the central carbon is only 3 carbons (propane), with two methyl substituents both on C2, giving 2,2-dimethylpropane.

questions.q: When two different numbering directions of the parent chain give the same lowest locant set, the tie is broken by giving the lower number to:
options: The substituent that comes first alphabetically
The substituent closer to C1 by default
The substituent mentioned last in the name
questions.expl: IUPAC rules break locant ties using alphabetical priority — whichever substituent is cited first alphabetically in the name gets the lower locant.

questions.q: A carbon atom attached to only one other carbon atom (e.g., a terminal CH<sub>3</sub>) is called:
questions.expl: Chain-end carbons and methyl branches, bonded to just one other carbon, are always primary.

questions.q: A quaternary (4°) carbon, such as the central carbon of neopentane, has how many hydrogen atoms attached to it?
questions.expl: A quaternary carbon is bonded to four other carbons, using up all four of its bonds, so it carries no hydrogen atoms at all.

questions.q: Since alkanes have no functional group, ring, or multiple bond to reposition, the only constitutional isomerism they can show is:
questions.expl: With nothing to reposition except the carbon skeleton itself, alkanes can only differ in how the chain is branched — chain/skeletal isomerism.

questions.q: How many structural isomers does butane (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) have?
questions.expl: Butane can only be arranged as a straight 4-carbon chain (n-butane) or with one branch (isobutane/2-methylpropane) — exactly 2 isomers.

questions.q: How many structural (chain) isomers does pentane (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>) have?
questions.expl: Pentane has 3 possible skeletons: the straight chain (n-pentane), one branch (isopentane/2-methylbutane), and the fully branched neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane).

questions.q: The degree of unsaturation of any open-chain alkane C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> is:
questions.expl: Degree of unsaturation = (2n+2 − 2n)/2 = 0 for every value of n, confirming alkanes have no rings or multiple bonds regardless of chain length.

questions.q: How many structurally distinct isomers do methane, ethane, and propane each have?
options: Just 1 each — branching isn't possible with 3 or fewer carbons
questions.expl: You need at least 4 carbons to have a branch point with a chain on either side, so methane, ethane, and propane can each only be drawn one way — chain isomerism starts at butane.

questions.q: Hexane (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>) has how many chain isomers in total?
questions.expl: Hexane has exactly 5 possible carbon skeletons — the isomer count grows quickly as chain length increases (2 for butane, 3 for pentane, 5 for hexane, 9 for heptane).

questions.q: In the Wurtz reaction, two molecules of an alkyl halide react with sodium metal in dry ether to give:
questions.expl: Sodium generates alkyl radicals from R–X which couple to form the symmetrical alkane R–R, releasing NaX.

questions.q: The Wurtz reaction is generally believed to proceed by a free-radical mechanism by default, but which alternative (ionic, S<sub>N</sub>2-type) mechanism has also been proposed?
options: R–X + 2Na → R:⁻ Na⁺ + NaX, then the carbanion R:⁻ attacks a second R–X in an S<sub>N</sub>2 step
Simple homolysis of R–X with no involvement of sodium at all
Direct addition of Na across the C–X bond without breaking it
A concerted six-membered pericyclic transition state
questions.expl: Two mechanisms have been suggested for Wurtz coupling: the default free-radical pathway, and an ionic pathway where Na first reduces R–X to give a carbanion (R:⁻ Na⁺) that then does a nucleophilic (S<sub>N</sub>2) displacement on a second molecule of R–X.

questions.q: Reactivity of an alkyl halide towards the Wurtz reaction (for a given alkyl group) follows the order:
questions.expl: A weaker, more easily broken C–X bond reacts faster; since bond strength falls C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I, reactivity in Wurtz coupling runs the other way: R–I is the fastest and R–F essentially doesn't react at all.

questions.q: When Zn dust (in THF) is used as the reducing metal instead of Na for a Wurtz-type coupling (2RX + Zn → R–R + ZnX₂), the reaction is specifically called the:
questions.expl: The mechanism is the same as the ordinary Wurtz reaction; only the metal is swapped for zinc, and this variant is named the Frankland reaction.

questions.q: The Wurtz–Fittig reaction couples an aryl halide with an alkyl halide using sodium in dry ether to give:
questions.expl: 2 Na + R–I + Br–C₆H₅ → R–C₆H₅ + NaBr + NaI: the Wurtz–Fittig reaction extends Wurtz-type coupling to make an alkyl-substituted benzene from an aryl halide plus an alkyl halide.

questions.q: The Fittig reaction couples two molecules of an aryl halide (e.g. chlorobenzene) with sodium in dry ether to give:
questions.expl: 2 C₆H₅–Cl + 2Na → C₆H₅–C₆H₅ + 2NaCl: this is simply the aryl–aryl version of the Wurtz coupling idea, giving a biaryl product.

questions.q: The Ullmann reaction couples two aryl halides (Ar–X, X = Cl, Br, I) using copper metal, and (unlike Wurtz) proceeds through:
options: Oxidative addition of Ar–X to Cu, followed by reductive elimination of the biaryl
Direct S<sub>N</sub>2 attack of one aryl halide on another
Protonation of the aryl halide by copper
questions.expl: Cu first inserts into the Ar–X bond (oxidative addition) to give Ar–Cu–X; a second equivalent of Ar–X then reacts and the aryl groups are reductively eliminated together as the biaryl Ar–Ar, regenerating CuX — this is explicitly not a free-radical mechanism.

questions.q: A key limitation of the Wurtz reaction is that treating two different alkyl halides R–X and R'–X together with sodium gives:
options: A statistical mixture of R–R, R'–R', and R–R'
Exclusively R–R with R'–X left unreacted
questions.expl: Because both alkyl radicals are generated together in solution and can combine with either partner, using two different halides gives an unavoidable statistical mixture of three coupling products — which is why Wurtz is used only to make symmetrical alkanes from a single halide.

questions.q: The most reliable method to prepare an unsymmetrical alkane R–R' cleanly (avoiding the statistical-mixture problem of Wurtz) is:
options: The plain Wurtz reaction on two different halides
Kolbe electrolysis of two different acid salts
questions.expl: Reacting a lithium dialkylcuprate (Gilman reagent, R₂CuLi) with a different alkyl halide R'–X selectively gives R–R', because the mechanism only uses one of the two alkyl groups on copper as the nucleophile.

questions.q: A lithium dialkylcuprate, R₂CuLi (the Gilman reagent), is prepared by treating an alkyl halide with lithium metal to form R–Li, then reacting this with:
questions.expl: R–X —Li→ R–Li —CuI (THF)→ R₂CuLi + LiI: the organolithium reagent first forms, and reaction with CuI (transmetallation) converts it into the organocuprate.

questions.q: In transmetallation, an organometallic compound transfers its alkyl group to a new metal when that new metal is:
options: More electronegative than the original metal
Less electronegative than the original metal
Exactly as electronegative as the original metal
Any metal at all, regardless of electronegativity
questions.expl: Transmetallation proceeds toward the less polar, more stable C–metal bond — so the alkyl group moves onto whichever metal is more electronegative (closer to carbon's own electronegativity, ≈2.5), e.g. Li (≈1.0) transfers its alkyl group to Cu (≈1.9).

questions.q: In the Corey–House reaction R₂CuLi + R'–X → R–R', the alkyl group on copper acts as a strong nucleophile and the reaction generally follows which mechanism?
options: S<sub>N</sub>2, so it works with methyl, 1°, and 2° (sometimes) alkyl halides but fails with 3° halides
S<sub>N</sub>1, so it works best with 3° halides
Free-radical substitution, unaffected by halide class
questions.expl: Because the carbanionic alkyl group on copper is a strong nucleophile that displaces the halide by back-side attack (S<sub>N</sub>2), tertiary alkyl halides give mostly elimination instead and are a poor substrate for this reaction; R' itself (on the halide) can be 1°, 2°, or even 3°.

questions.q: A major advantage of organocuprates over simple Grignard or organolithium reagents in substitution reactions is that organocuprates can also react cleanly with:
options: Vinylic and aryl halides, which don't undergo S<sub>N</sub>2 with Grignard/organolithium reagents
No halides other than simple 1° alkyl halides
questions.expl: Vinylic and aryl C–X bonds resist ordinary nucleophilic (S<sub>N</sub>2/S<sub>N</sub>1) attack, but organocuprates react with them anyway (through a different, non-S<sub>N</sub>2 pathway at the metal), letting Corey–House build alkyl-substituted alkenes and arenes that Wurtz-type methods cannot.

questions.q: When an organocuprate reacts with a vinylic halide, the configuration of the starting alkene (cis or trans) in the product is:
options: Scrambled into a mixture of cis and trans
questions.expl: The substitution at the sp² vinylic carbon is stereospecific: the groups on the double bond keep their relative positions, so a cis-alkenyl halide gives a cis-alkene product and a trans-alkenyl halide gives a trans-alkene product.

questions.q: Besides plain alkyl/vinylic/aryl halides, organocuprates (R₂CuLi) can also substitute a leaving group on compounds bearing other functional groups, such as an acid halide, to directly give a:
options: Alkane only, with the functional group destroyed
questions.expl: R₂CuLi reacts with an acyl (acid) halide by replacing the halide with one R group, giving a ketone — organocuprates are mild and selective enough to leave the carbonyl itself untouched while only the leaving group is substituted.

questions.q: Heating the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda-lime (NaOH + CaO) gives the alkane with one fewer carbon. This reaction is called:
questions.expl: R–COONa + NaOH —(CaO, Δ)→ R–H + Na₂CO₃: soda-lime decarboxylation removes –COONa as Na₂CO₃, leaving the alkane R–H.

questions.q: In the soda-lime decarboxylation reaction, what role does the CaO actually play in the chemistry (as opposed to NaOH)?
options: No direct chemical role — CaO is just mixed in because it's cheaper and easier to handle than pure solid NaOH
CaO is the actual base that removes CO₂
CaO reduces the carbon chain by one more carbon
CaO oxidizes the carboxylate to CO₂ directly
questions.expl: NaOH alone does the decarboxylation chemistry. CaO is added because pure solid NaOH is hygroscopic and corrosive to handle, while soda-lime (NaOH + CaO, 3:1) is a much easier, cheaper solid to work with, and CaO conveniently also absorbs atmospheric CO₂ and water like NaOH does.

questions.q: Decarboxylation of a carboxylate proceeds via loss of CO₂ to generate a carbanion in the rate-determining step. Therefore, decarboxylation is faster (more favorable) when the resulting carbanion is:
options: More stable (e.g., stabilized by nearby electron-withdrawing groups)
Exactly as stable regardless of substituents
questions.expl: Since the C–C bond breaks heterolytically to form a carbanion in the slow step, any factor that stabilizes that carbanion (such as a nearby electron-withdrawing/nitro group, or aromatic/allylic delocalization) speeds up decarboxylation.

questions.q: If a carboxylic acid or its salt has an electron-withdrawing group at the β-position relative to –COOH, decarboxylation can occur:
options: Simply on heating, without needing soda-lime at all
Only with soda-lime and never by heating alone
Not at all, since EWGs block decarboxylation
questions.expl: A β-electron-withdrawing group (as in β-keto acids) stabilizes the developing carbanion/enolate so effectively that simple heating alone is enough to drive off CO₂, without requiring the soda-lime reagent.

questions.q: Decarboxylation of sodium benzoate (C₆H₅COONa) with soda-lime gives:
questions.expl: C₆H₅COONa + NaOH —(CaO,Δ)→ C₆H₆ + Na₂CO₃ — removing the –COONa group from the aromatic ring leaves plain benzene, <svg viewBox="0 0 120 110" width="22" height="20" style="vertical-align:middle;margin:0 3px;"><polygon points="60,13 96,34 96,76 60,97 24,76 24,34" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="7"/><circle cx="60" cy="55" r="24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="5"/></svg> benzene.

questions.q: Kolbe's electrolytic method makes a symmetrical alkane by electrolysing a concentrated aqueous solution of a carboxylate salt. At the anode, the mechanism proceeds as:
options: 2RCOO⁻ directly gains electrons to form R–R
R–R forms by simple ionic combination of two RCOO⁻ ions
CO₂ and R–R form only at the cathode
questions.expl: At the anode the carboxylate loses an electron to form a carboxyl radical, which rapidly loses CO₂ to give an alkyl radical; two such alkyl radicals then combine to give the symmetrical alkane R–R.

questions.q: In Kolbe's electrolysis, what happens at the cathode?
options: The carboxylate is reduced directly to the alkane
CO₂ is generated at the cathode instead of the anode
Nothing — the cathode is inert in this reaction
questions.expl: While decarboxylation and radical coupling happen at the anode, the cathode simply reduces water, liberating H₂ gas and regenerating NaOH in solution.

questions.q: Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene or alkyne with H₂ over Ni, Pd, or Pt is:
options: Exothermic only for alkynes, endothermic for alkenes
questions.expl: Hydrogenation is exothermic because the new, strong C–H and additional C–C σ-bonds formed release more energy than is needed to break the weaker H–H and π-bonds.

questions.q: In catalytic hydrogenation, the metal surface's real role is to:
options: Adsorb both H₂ and the alkene/alkyne, lowering the activation energy and enabling syn addition of the two H atoms from the same face
Act as a Lewis acid that polarizes the C=C bond
Supply electrons for an S<sub>N</sub>1-type mechanism
Oxidize the alkene before H₂ is added
questions.expl: H₂ and the unsaturated substrate are both adsorbed onto the metal surface, and both hydrogen atoms are delivered to the same face of the double/triple bond, giving syn (cis) addition, with the metal lowering the overall activation energy of the reaction.

questions.q: Raney nickel is prepared by treating a nickel–aluminium alloy with:
options: Concentrated NaOH, which dissolves out the aluminium as sodium aluminate, leaving a highly porous, catalytically active nickel
Dilute HCl, which dissolves the nickel
Heating the alloy alone with no other reagent
Concentrated H₂SO₄, which dissolves both metals
questions.expl: Ni–Al alloy + NaOH removes the aluminium (as soluble sodium aluminate), leaving behind a spongy, high-surface-area nickel that is an excellent hydrogenation catalyst.

questions.q: Catalytic hydrogenation of a cis-alkene by syn addition, when it creates two new similar stereocentres with no other pre-existing chiral centre, gives:
questions.expl: Because both new H atoms add from the same face (syn addition) and the alkene was cis, the two new stereocentres end up with an internal mirror plane, producing the achiral meso diastereomer as a single compound.

questions.q: Under the same syn-addition conditions, hydrogenating the corresponding trans-alkene (in place of the cis one above) instead gives:
options: An achiral product with no stereocentres
questions.expl: Starting from the trans-alkene, syn addition places the two new stereocentres without the internal mirror symmetry the cis-alkene gave, producing the two enantiomers in equal (racemic) amounts instead of the single meso compound.

questions.q: In terms of ease of catalytic hydrogenation, greater steric crowding around the double/triple bond makes the reaction rate:
options: Lower — rate is inversely related to steric crowding
Dependent only on the catalyst, never on the substrate
questions.expl: More heavily substituted (bulkier) alkenes/alkynes have more trouble adsorbing flat against the catalyst surface, so the rate of catalytic hydrogenation is roughly proportional to 1/(steric crowding) — a terminal, unhindered double bond hydrogenates fastest.

questions.q: Which is generally true when comparing catalysts for the same substrate?
options: Raney nickel gives a faster rate of hydrogenation than plain Ni/H₂
Plain Ni/H₂ is always faster than Raney nickel
Both give identical rates in all cases
questions.expl: Because Raney nickel is far more finely divided and porous (much higher effective surface area) than ordinary nickel, it hydrogenates a given substrate faster under comparable conditions.

questions.q: Hydrogenating an alkyne over Lindlar's catalyst (Pd deposited on CaCO₃ or BaSO₄, poisoned with a lead salt/quinoline) stops at the alkene stage and delivers H₂ by:
options: Syn addition, giving the cis-alkene as the major product
Radical addition, giving a mixture of cis and trans
No addition — Lindlar's catalyst is inactive toward alkynes
questions.expl: The catalyst poison (quinoline, or a lead salt like lead acetate) deliberately lowers the catalyst's activity just enough to stop hydrogenation at the alkene stage; both H atoms still add from the same face (syn addition), so the alkyne is converted to the cis-alkene.

questions.q: Nickel boride (Ni₂B, the "P-2 catalyst") is another catalyst used to partially reduce alkynes to alkenes; like Lindlar's catalyst, it proceeds by:
options: A free-radical mechanism giving trans-alkene as major product
Full reduction straight to the alkane
questions.expl: Ni₂B (P-2 catalyst) is a milder alternative to Lindlar's catalyst that similarly delivers both hydrogens from the same face of the alkyne, also stopping cleanly at the cis-alkene.

questions.q: Reducing an alkyne with Na (or Li) dissolved in liquid NH₃ (Birch-type conditions) gives the corresponding alkene by:
options: Anti addition, giving the trans-alkene as the major product
No reaction — alkynes are inert to dissolving-metal conditions
questions.expl: This dissolving-metal reduction proceeds through a vinyl radical/vinyl anion sequence (electron transfer, protonation, second electron transfer, second protonation) rather than on a metal surface, and delivers the two H atoms from opposite faces — anti addition — giving predominantly the more stable trans-alkene.

questions.q: In the Na/liquid-NH₃ reduction of an internal alkyne, the mechanism generates a vinyl radical intermediate that is then converted to the alkene product via:
options: A second electron transfer to give a vinyl anion, followed by protonation by the solvent (NH₃)
Direct H–H addition from molecular hydrogen
Direct protonation of the vinyl radical without any further electron transfer
questions.expl: The sequence is: alkyne + e⁻ → radical anion → protonation → vinyl radical + e⁻ → vinyl anion → protonation (by NH₃) → alkene; the trans geometry is favoured because the more stable, less hindered vinyl radical/anion intermediate forms preferentially.

questions.q: Diimide (HN=NH), generated in situ, selectively reduces alkenes and alkynes (nonpolar, symmetrical multiple bonds) but does not touch polar multiple bonds like C=O or C=N because:
options: Diimide is short-lived and self-destructs to N₂ + hydrazine before it can react with the less-reactive polar bonds
Polar bonds are inherently stronger than C=C or C≡C bonds
Diimide only reacts under strongly acidic conditions, which polar bonds don't tolerate
Diimide preferentially reduces only aromatic rings
questions.expl: Diimide is a fleeting reactive species that disproportionates to N₂ and N₂H₄ if it doesn't react immediately; this short lifetime makes it selective for the fast-reacting nonpolar π-systems (C=C, C≡C, N=N) while sparing the slower-reacting polar C=O/C=N bonds.

questions.q: Diimide reduces a C=C double bond through a pericyclic mechanism involving:
options: A six-membered cyclic transition state, giving syn addition of both H atoms with loss of N₂
Sequential one-electron transfers, like the Birch reduction
Simple ionic addition of H⁺ and H⁻
questions.expl: Diimide and the alkene come together in a concerted, six-membered cyclic transition state (bonds breaking and forming simultaneously); both H atoms are delivered to the same face of the double bond (syn addition) as N₂ is expelled.

questions.q: Diimide can be generated in situ for use as a reducing agent from hydrazine (N₂H₄) by treating it with:
options: An oxidant such as H₂O₂ or O₂ (or light, hν)
A strong reducing agent like LiAlH₄
questions.expl: N₂H₄ + H₂O₂ (or O₂, or another oxidant, sometimes with light) oxidizes hydrazine just enough to form the reactive diimide HN=NH in solution, ready to reduce a nearby alkene/alkyne.

questions.q: Clemmensen reduction converts an aldehyde or ketone carbonyl fully to a CH₂/CH₃ group using:
options: Zn–Hg amalgam with concentrated HCl (acidic conditions)
NH₂–NH₂ with KOH in ethylene glycol (basic conditions)
Ethanedithiol followed by Raney nickel (neutral conditions)
questions.expl: R–CHO/R–CO–R' + Zn(Hg)/HCl, Δ → R–CH₃/R–CH₂–R' + ZnCl₂ + H₂O; Clemmensen reduction runs in strongly acidic conditions and is chosen when the rest of the molecule can tolerate acid but not base.

questions.q: Wolff–Kishner reduction converts a carbonyl to a CH₂/CH₃ group by first forming a hydrazone (R₂C=N–NH₂) and then heating it with KOH in ethylene glycol. This reaction runs in:
options: Basic conditions, and is chosen when the substrate is acid-sensitive
Acidic conditions, chosen for base-sensitive substrates
questions.expl: Because Wolff–Kishner uses hydrazine and hot base rather than acid, it's the reduction of choice for substrates bearing base-tolerant but acid-sensitive functional groups — the opposite scenario to Clemmensen.

questions.q: In the exceptional case of Clemmensen-reducing a 1,3-diketone such as 5,5-dimethylcyclohexane-1,3-dione, the major product is not the expected 1,1-dimethylcyclohexane but instead a ring-contracted methyl ketone. This happens because:
options: An intermediate carbocation undergoes a 1,2-alkyl shift (ring contraction) before the second carbonyl is fully reduced
The acidic medium hydrolyses the ring completely
HCl adds across the ring without reducing either carbonyl
questions.expl: Partial reduction/dehydration of one carbonyl generates a cationic intermediate; rather than simply completing reduction, a neighbouring C–C bond migrates (1,2-alkyl shift), contracting the six-membered ring to a five-membered one and giving 2,4,4-trimethylcyclopentanone as the major product.

questions.q: The Mozingo reduction converts a ketone/aldehyde to a CH₂ group by first forming a cyclic dithioacetal (using ethane-1,2-dithiol and dry HCl) and then desulfurizing it with:
questions.expl: The carbonyl is first protected as a 1,3-dithiolane, then Raney nickel (which is loaded with adsorbed hydrogen) reductively cleaves both C–S bonds, replacing the ring with two C–H bonds — an essentially neutral-condition alternative to Clemmensen/Wolff–Kishner.

questions.q: Compared to Clemmensen (strongly acidic) and Wolff–Kishner (strongly basic) conditions, the Mozingo reduction is especially useful when the rest of the molecule contains a group that is:
options: Sensitive to both strong acid and strong base
questions.expl: Because the dithioacetal-formation and Raney-nickel desulfurization steps avoid strongly acidic or strongly basic conditions, Mozingo reduction is the fallback method when a substrate can't survive either of the other two carbonyl-reduction methods.

questions.q: Treating an alcohol (R–OH) with excess HI in the presence of red phosphorus (as a catalyst/HI regenerator) at elevated temperature ultimately gives:
options: The alkyl iodide, R–I, with no further reaction
No reaction — alcohols are inert to HI/red P
questions.expl: HI/red P first converts –OH to –I (red P regenerates HI from the I₂ byproduct, keeping the reagent in excess), and then, under forcing/excess conditions, further reduces the C–I bond itself, ultimately replacing the original –OH with plain –H.

questions.q: HI/red phosphorus is considered an unusually powerful, "exhaustive" reducing combination because, given excess reagent and heat, it can even reduce a ketone/aldehyde carbonyl all the way down to a simple CH₂/CH₃ group by:
options: First converting the C=O to a C–I (via the alcohol) and then reducing that C–I bond to C–H
Directly inserting H₂ across the C=O in one step
Oxidizing the carbonyl to a carboxylic acid first
Leaving carbonyls completely untouched under all conditions
questions.expl: HI/red P can first reduce the carbonyl to the alcohol and then to the alkyl iodide, and finally reduce that C–I bond too — which is why it's grouped with Clemmensen/Wolff–Kishner/Mozingo as one of the standard ways to fully deoxygenate a carbonyl to a CH₂/CH₃ group.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of aluminium carbide, Al₄C₃, with water gives:
questions.expl: Al₄C₃ + 12H₂O → 4Al(OH)₃ + 3CH₄: aluminium carbide is a "methanide" and its hydrolysis is a classic laboratory preparation of methane.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of calcium carbide, CaC₂, with water gives:
questions.expl: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂: calcium carbide is an "acetylide" (contains the C≡C²⁻ unit) and its hydrolysis is the classic industrial/lab route to acetylene, not an alkane — a common point of confusion with methanide carbides like Al₄C₃ or Be₂C.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of beryllium carbide, Be₂C, with water gives:
questions.expl: Be₂C + 2H₂O → 2Be(OH)₂ + CH₄: like Al₄C₃, beryllium carbide is a methanide, giving methane on hydrolysis.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of magnesium carbide, Mg₂C₃ (a so-called "allylenide"), with water gives:
questions.expl: Mg₂C₃ + 4H₂O → 2Mg(OH)₂ + CH₃–C≡CH: this carbide contains a three-carbon unit and hydrolyses specifically to propyne, unlike the two-carbon acetylide (CaC₂) or one-carbon methanide (Al₄C₃/Be₂C) carbides.

questions.q: Treating a Grignard reagent (R–MgX) with water (or any active-hydrogen compound) gives:
questions.expl: The polarized, basic C–Mg bond is protonated by even a weak acid like water, quenching it to R–H + Mg(OH)X — which is why Grignard reactions must be kept rigorously moisture-free until this quenching step is actually wanted.

questions.q: Among Al₄C₃, CaC₂, Be₂C, and Mg₂C₃, the carbides that give methane (rather than an alkyne) on hydrolysis are:
questions.expl: Al₄C₃ and Be₂C are both "methanides" (isolated C⁴⁻ centres) and hydrolyse to methane, while CaC₂ (an acetylide, C₂²⁻) gives acetylene and Mg₂C₃ (an allylenide, C₃⁴⁻) gives propyne — the carbide's structure, not just "any carbide," determines the hydrolysis product.

questions.q: Among isomeric alkanes, increasing the amount of branching generally makes the boiling point:
questions.expl: Branching makes a molecule more compact and spherical, shrinking its surface area of contact with neighbouring molecules and weakening van der Waals forces — so isobutane boils lower than n-butane.

questions.q: Alkanes are essentially _____ in water and _____ in nonpolar organic solvents like benzene.
questions.expl: Nonpolar C–H/C–C bonds can't hydrogen-bond with water, so alkanes are hydrophobic, but they dissolve readily in nonpolar solvents ("like dissolves like").

questions.q: At room temperature, the first four alkanes (methane through butane) exist as:
questions.expl: C₁–C₄ alkanes are gases at room temperature; roughly C₅–C₁₇ are liquids, and heavier alkanes are waxy solids.

questions.q: Compared to water, the density of liquid alkanes is:
questions.expl: Liquid alkanes are typically around 0.6–0.8 g/mL, well below water's 1.0 g/mL, which is why spilled oil/hydrocarbons float on water.

questions.q: In the alternating melting-point trend of the n-alkane series, alkanes with an even number of carbons tend to have _____ melting points than neighbouring odd-carbon alkanes.
questions.expl: Even-carbon chains pack more symmetrically into the crystal lattice than odd-chain ones of similar length, giving them a modestly higher melting point and producing the characteristic zig-zag (odd-even) trend.

questions.q: The intermolecular forces responsible for holding pure liquid/solid alkanes together are exclusively:
questions.expl: With no polar bonds or lone pairs available for hydrogen bonding or significant dipole–dipole interaction, only weak, universal London dispersion forces hold alkane molecules to one another — which is also why their boiling points are relatively low for their molecular size.

questions.q: The three mechanistic steps of free-radical halogenation of an alkane, in the correct order, are:
questions.expl: The chain reaction must first generate radicals (initiation), then repeatedly consume/regenerate them to build product (propagation), and finally radicals combine to end the chain (termination).

questions.q: The initiation step of the radical chlorination of methane involves:
options: Homolytic fission of Cl₂ by heat or UV light into 2 Cl•
Heterolytic fission of Cl₂ into Cl⁺ and Cl⁻
Direct addition of Cl₂ across a C–H bond
Formation of CH₃Cl in a single step
questions.expl: Light or heat supplies just enough energy to homolytically cleave the relatively weak Cl–Cl bond into two chlorine radicals, which then go on to propagate the chain.

questions.q: The rate of H-atom abstraction from a C–H bond during radical halogenation follows the order:
options: All C–H bonds react at the same rate
questions.expl: More substituted radicals are more stable (hyperconjugation and inductive donation from alkyl groups), lowering the transition-state energy for their formation, so abstraction is fastest at tertiary C–H bonds.

questions.q: Reactivity of the halogens toward alkanes in radical halogenation follows the order:
questions.expl: F₂ reacts almost explosively (highly exothermic, poorly selective), Cl₂ reacts readily, Br₂ is slower but far more selective, and I₂ barely reacts at all (the H-abstraction step is endothermic) unless an oxidizer removes the HI formed.

questions.q: Compared to chlorination, bromination of an alkane is:
options: More selective for the more substituted (e.g., tertiary) C–H bond
questions.expl: Because H-abstraction by Br• is endothermic, its transition state resembles the product radical more closely (Hammond postulate), making bromination far more sensitive to radical stability and hence much more selective for tertiary over primary C–H bonds than chlorination.

questions.q: Which termination step is possible in the radical chlorination of methane?
options: Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂, or CH₃• + CH₃• → CHゃ–CHゃ, or CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl
Only Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂ is possible
Only CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl is possible
Termination cannot occur once the chain has started
questions.expl: Termination consumes radicals without producing more, and any two radicals present in solution can combine — giving Cl₂ back, a small amount of ethane as a side-product, or CH₃Cl directly.

questions.q: Complete combustion of an alkane in excess oxygen produces:
questions.expl: With ample O₂, every carbon is fully oxidized to CO₂ and every hydrogen ends up as H₂O, releasing a large amount of heat.

questions.q: When the oxygen supply is limited, combustion of an alkane can instead produce:
questions.expl: Under O₂-starved conditions the carbon isn't fully oxidized, so incomplete combustion yields carbon monoxide or even unburned soot alongside water.

questions.q: Thermal decomposition of higher alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes at high temperature (≈773 K) in the absence of air is called:
questions.expl: Cracking proceeds via a free-radical mechanism and is used industrially to break heavier petroleum fractions down into more valuable lighter fractions such as gasoline.

questions.q: Heating n-hexane over a catalyst such as Cr₂O₃/Al₂O₃ (or Pt) at high temperature and pressure to form benzene is an example of:
questions.expl: This cyclization-plus-dehydrogenation converts a straight-chain C₆ (or higher) alkane into an aromatic ring, <svg viewBox="0 0 120 110" width="22" height="20" style="vertical-align:middle;margin:0 3px;"><polygon points="60,13 96,34 96,76 60,97 24,76 24,34" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="7"/><circle cx="60" cy="55" r="24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="5"/></svg> benzene, and is used industrially to raise the octane number of petrol.

questions.q: Treating n-butane with anhydrous AlCl₃/HCl converts it into isobutane. This rearrangement is called:
questions.expl: Isomerization rearranges a straight-chain alkane into a more branched isomer without changing the molecular formula, which raises the octane rating of the fuel.

questions.q: Passing a lower alkane/air mixture over a catalyst (e.g. Cu or Mo₂O₃) under controlled temperature and pressure, so that it is only partially oxidized instead of fully combusted, can give:
options: Alcohols, aldehydes, or carboxylic acids depending on conditions
Exclusively CO₂ and H₂O, same as combustion
