questions.expl: Controlled catalytic oxidation deliberately stops short of full combustion, giving industrially useful oxygenated products (alcohols/aldehydes/acids) from cheap alkane feedstocks instead of just heat.

questions.q: Rotation about the C–C single bond in ethane gives infinite arrangements; the two extreme (limiting) forms are called:
questions.expl: Staggered (front and back C–H bonds 60° apart) and eclipsed (bonds directly aligned, 0° apart) are the two limiting conformations of ethane; chair/boat describe cyclic systems, not open-chain ethane.

questions.q: Which conformation of ethane is more stable, and why?
options: Staggered — it minimizes torsional strain between the C–H bonding electrons
Eclipsed — the aligned bonds stabilize each other
Staggered — due to steric bulk of the hydrogens
questions.expl: In the staggered form the C–H bonding pairs on the front and back carbons are as far apart as possible, minimizing torsional (Pitzer) strain from their electron-electron repulsion, making staggered the lowest-energy, most populated conformation.

questions.q: The rotational energy barrier in ethane (staggered → eclipsed) is approximately:
questions.expl: This small barrier, arising purely from torsional strain (ethane has no bulky substituents), is easily overcome by thermal energy at room temperature, so conformers interconvert rapidly and cannot be isolated as separate compounds.

questions.q: Conformational isomers differ from constitutional/configurational isomers in that conformers:
options: Interconvert by rotation about a single bond without breaking any bonds
Can only interconvert by breaking and reforming bonds
Are non-superimposable mirror images of each other
Differ in the position of a functional group on the chain
questions.expl: Because conformers are related purely by free rotation around a σ-bond, they aren't isolable as distinct compounds the way constitutional or configurational isomers are.

questions.q: A Newman projection is drawn by viewing the molecule:
options: Along the axis of the C–C bond, so the front carbon is a dot and the rear carbon is a circle
Perpendicular to the C–C bond, as a wedge-dash structure
From above, as in a Fischer projection
questions.expl: Looking straight down the C–C bond, front-atom bonds are drawn radiating from a central point and back-atom bonds radiate from the edge of a circle behind it, making the dihedral (torsional) angle between them easy to read off.

questions.q: Because ethane rotates freely between conformations at room temperature and they interconvert far faster than they can be separated, staggered and eclipsed ethane are best described as:
options: The same compound in different conformations, not different compounds
questions.expl: Since no bond is broken during the interconversion and the energy barrier is easily crossed at room temperature, staggered and eclipsed ethane are simply different snapshots of one and the same molecule, not separate compounds.

questions.q: n-Butane is converted to isobutane at 400°C using which reagent?
questions.expl: Isomerization of an unbranched alkane to its more stable branched isomer is done by heating with anhydrous AlCl3 and HCl (general form AlX3 + HX).

questions.q: n-Heptane isomerizes into its most stable branched form, known by which trivial name?
questions.expl: n-Heptane converts into 2,2,3-trimethylbutane, whose trivial name is triptane.

questions.q: n-Hexane heated at 773 K, 10-20 atm over Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>-Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> gives mainly:
questions.expl: Aromatization (reforming) dehydrogenates and cyclizes n-hexane specifically into benzene; n-heptane instead gives toluene, and n-octane gives o-xylene/ethylbenzene.

questions.q: What does the aromatization/reforming reaction achieve, industrially?
options: Converts aliphatic hydrocarbons to aromatic ones to raise octane number
Converts branched alkanes to unbranched ones
Cracks heavy oil into lighter fractions
questions.expl: Reforming converts straight-chain aliphatic alkanes into aromatic rings (benzene/toluene/xylenes), which have a higher octane number, improving fuel quality.

questions.q: Why can alkanes generally not be reduced further?
options: Their carbons are already at the minimum oxidation state
questions.expl: Since alkane carbons already sit at their minimum oxidation state, further reduction is not possible.

questions.q: Which C-H bond in an alkane is oxidized directly by hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> (Baeyer's reagent) to give an alcohol?
options: None — alkanes never react with KMnO4
questions.expl: A tertiary C-H has enough electron density (similar to alkene/alkyne C-H) to be oxidized by hot KMnO4 directly to the corresponding tertiary alcohol; this is the one exception to alkanes resisting oxidation.

questions.q: Why does cyclopropane give addition reactions, unlike other alkanes?
options: Its ring strain (60° bond angles) makes it highly reactive
It has an odd number of carbons
questions.expl: Cyclopropane's bond angles are compressed to 60 degrees instead of the ideal 109.5 degrees, creating severe angle strain that makes the ring open readily via addition.

questions.q: Cyclopropane + H<sub>2</sub>/Ni at 80°C gives:
questions.expl: Catalytic hydrogenation of cyclopropane's strained ring gives straight-chain propane.

questions.q: What is the molecularity/order of a typical E2 dehydrohalogenation reaction?
questions.expl: E2 rate = k[substrate][base], so it is second order overall (bimolecular), consistent with its single concerted step.

questions.q: Which transition-state geometry does E2 elimination require?
questions.expl: E2 proceeds through a single-step, anti-periplanar transition state — also referred to as anti-elimination.

questions.q: Why does R-F often go through E1cB instead of E2?
options: Fluoride is too good a leaving group
Fluoride is a poor leaving group, so deprotonation happens first
questions.expl: Since F- is a poor leaving group, the beta-H is removed first to form a carbanion (especially if stabilized by an EWG/conjugating group), and loss of fluoride follows — this is the E1cB pathway.

questions.q: An E2 reaction on a substrate with chiral alpha and beta carbons is:
questions.expl: E2 is stereospecific when both the alpha and beta carbons are chiral centres, since the anti-periplanar requirement fixes the relative geometry of the product.

questions.q: With an unsymmetrical substrate and a non-bulky strong base, E2 elimination gives mainly the:
questions.expl: With an ordinary (non-bulky) strong base, the more substituted, more stable alkene forms preferentially — the Zaitsev (Saytzeff) rule.

questions.q: Which of these bases favours the Hofmann (less substituted) elimination product?
questions.expl: Bulky bases like potassium/sodium tert-butoxide (and LDA) remove the least hindered beta-H, favouring the less substituted Hofmann product.

questions.q: If the beta-carbon of an alkyl halide is attached to a phenyl group, the major elimination product is:
options: Always the Hofmann product, regardless of base
The conjugated (phenyl-stabilized) alkene, even with a bulky base
questions.expl: Conjugation with phenyl (or vinyl) stabilizes the resulting alkene strongly enough that it remains the major product even when a bulky, Hofmann-favouring base is used.

questions.q: What three roles does H2SO4 play in the acid-catalyzed dehydration of an alcohol?
questions.expl: H2SO4 in this reaction acts simultaneously as the catalyst, the acid, and the dehydrating agent (H3PO4 or KHSO4 can be substituted for the same purpose).

questions.q: Rank the reactivity of alcohols toward acid-catalyzed (E1) dehydration.
questions.expl: Since the RDS involves carbocation formation, more substituted (more stable) carbocations form faster, so reactivity follows 3 degree > 2 degree > 1 degree alcohols.

questions.q: In the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst (e.g. Al2O3, P2O5), alcohol dehydration proceeds mainly through which mechanism?
questions.expl: Lewis acids like P2O5, Al2O3, ThO2, or POCl3 push alcohol dehydration through the E2 mechanism, unlike protonic acids which favour E1.

questions.q: Why must rearrangement always be considered in acid-catalyzed alcohol dehydration?
options: The RDS generates a carbocation intermediate
questions.expl: Because the rate-determining step forms a carbocation, hydride/alkyl shifts or ring expansion/contraction are always a possibility that must be checked for.

questions.q: Zn/AcOH converts a vicinal dihalide into an alkene by:
options: Donating 2 electrons that expel both halides at once
questions.expl: Zn is oxidized to Zn2+, donating two electrons that are used to expel both halide ions from the adjacent carbons in one concerted step, forming the alkene.

questions.q: What drives the NaI/acetone dehalogenation of a vicinal dihalide to completion?
options: Precipitation of NaBr (or KBr) out of acetone
The reaction doesn't need driving — it's spontaneous
questions.expl: NaBr/KBr is insoluble in acetone and precipitates out, pulling the equilibrium toward the elimination product — the same driving force behind the Finkelstein reaction.

questions.q: Dehalogenation eliminations of vicinal dihalides (Zn, Mg, or NaI routes) proceed through which geometry?
questions.expl: Like E2, these dehalogenation eliminations require an anti-coplanar arrangement of the two leaving halogens.

questions.q: What defines a ylide?
options: A compound with formal positive and negative charges on adjacent atoms, net neutral
A carbanion with no charge separation
A compound with two positive charges
questions.expl: A ylide carries formal positive and negative charges on adjacent atoms while being overall neutral in charge — phosphorus, nitrogen, and sulfur ylides are the common types.

questions.q: In the Wittig reaction, a ketone reacts with a phosphorus ylide to give an alkene plus which byproduct?
questions.expl: R2C=O + Ph3P=CH2 gives the new alkene R2C=CH2 along with triphenylphosphine oxide, O=PPh3, as the byproduct.

questions.q: What is the main synthetic value of the Wittig reaction?
options: It converts a carbonyl group directly into a C=C bond at a defined position
questions.expl: Unlike elimination reactions, which can give a mixture of alkene regiochemistries, the Wittig reaction installs the new double bond at exactly the carbon that carried the carbonyl.

questions.q: Why does dehydrohalogenation of a vicinal dihalide with alcoholic KOH often stop at the vinyl halide stage?
options: Vinyl halides are very unreactive to further mild elimination
The reaction is complete after one HX loss
Vinyl halides can't lose more HX under any conditions
KOH only removes one equivalent of HX ever
questions.expl: The C-X bond in a vinyl halide is much less reactive under mild conditions, so a stronger base (like NaNH2) and more vigorous conditions are needed to remove the second HX and reach the alkyne.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of CaC2 (calcium carbide) gives:
questions.expl: CaC2 contains the acetylide C2(2-) unit, so its hydrolysis gives ethyne (HC≡CH) + Ca(OH)2 + heat.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of Al4C3 (aluminium carbide) gives which gas?
questions.expl: Al4C3 is a methanide-type carbide (isolated carbon, not an acetylide unit), so its hydrolysis gives methane, not an alkyne.

questions.q: Berthelot's synthesis of ethyne combines carbon and hydrogen using:
questions.expl: Berthelot's synthesis passes an electric arc between carbon electrodes in a hydrogen atmosphere at around 1200 degrees C to give ethyne directly.

questions.q: A terminal alkyne with ammoniacal AgNO3 (Tollen's reagent) gives:
options: A red precipitate of copper acetylide
A white precipitate of silver acetylide
questions.expl: Terminal alkynes give a white precipitate of the silver acetylide (R-C≡C-Ag) with ammoniacal AgNO3; internal alkynes give no such precipitate.

questions.q: Why is the silver/copper acetylide test diagnostic specifically for terminal alkynes?
options: Only terminal alkynes have an acidic C-H that the metal ion can displace
questions.expl: Only a terminal alkyne has a C-H directly on the triple bond acidic enough to be displaced by Ag+ or Cu+, forming the insoluble acetylide; internal alkynes have no such C-H.

questions.q: Treating a 2-alkyne with NaNH2 in liquid NH3 shifts it toward the:
questions.expl: NaNH2, a strong base, deprotonates the terminal-most acidic position to form the stable acetylide anion; since this removes the terminal alkyne from equilibrium, the reaction drives essentially to completion toward the 1-alkyne (Le Chatelier's principle).

questions.q: To build a higher, unsymmetrical alkyne from a terminal alkyne, the correct sequence is:
options: Form the sodium acetylide with Na/NH3, then alkylate with a primary R-X
Add HBr, then eliminate with KOH
questions.expl: The terminal alkyne is first converted to its sodium acetylide (Na, liquid NH3), which then reacts via SN2 with a primary alkyl halide to build the new, longer alkyne chain.
